newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania presidential poll essential for economy.
newsitem.headline: Romania presidential poll essential for economy.

text.p: Romanian voters choose this weekend between an incumbent president who has stuck to cautious reforms or his centrist rival who wants a free hand to hoist the country out of its economic chasm.

President Ion Iliescu, in power since the 1989 fall of communism, goes into Sunday's run-off presidential election saying he favours faster reforms, but admits he has sought to cushion Romanians against austerity measures.
Emil Constantinescu, four points behind Iliescu in the first round, says such reluctance has "exhausted" Romanians and widened the gap with ex-Communist states Poland and Hungary.

He wants to start a countdown to fulfil campaign promises -- tax cuts and improved benefits combined with financial and budget discipline -- after his Democratic Convention (CDR) routed Iliescu's party in parliamentary polls this month.
"So far the reform has meant sacrifice for the people's sake and people being sacrificed for the sake of reform," Constantinescu said this week.
The most important thing, he said, was to get on with the business of government. "Romania needs government quickly, it does not need endless haggling, confusion and chaos." he said.

Regardless of the outcome, the new government will be drawn mainly from Constantinescu's CDR and the Social Democrats of former Prime Minister Petre Roman, who backs his presidential bid after coming third in the opening round.

The CDR fought its campaign on a "Contract with Romania" which commits the government to meet targets within 200 days. Constantinescu says electing him gives him a mandate to act on reforms and rid Romania of the last vestiges of its past.

Iliescu pledges to work with the government while acting to counterbalance a legislature and cabinet run by his opponents. "I will temper excesses and oppose any tendency to make tradeoffs in the country's serious problems," he told voters.

The president has considerable weight in determining the shape and speed of policy. He promulgates laws, appoints part of the board of the country's main privatisation body and can summon parliamentary commissions to debate economic issues.
"The outcome is extremely important as in the existing structure the president can operate important levers in the economy," economist Teodor Nicolaescu said.
"A president with a political outlook different from that of the parliamentary majority has to cooperate with a government pursuing a policy he does not embrace."

Economists say budgetary and currency issues must be tackled promptly to contain inflation now running at 45 percent, resume suspended credits from the International Monetary Fund and gain more credibility from foreign investors.
The budget deficit surged to 2.86 trillion lei in nine months and is seen ballooning to 4.27 trillion by end-1996.

Romania will also have to re-examine its foreign exchange markets. The leu currency has sunk in the past month from 3,500 to 4,900 to the dollar at retail shops, while government policy props it at 38 percent higher on the interbank market.
All that will mean taking unpopular steps, including energy price rises, allowing the leu to slide to its true value on currency markets and forcing industry to pay bills on time.
Iliescu dismisses the CDR economic plan as unworkable and too expensive at the equivalent of $1.45 billion per year.

"The CDR has a political programme of demagoguery. Who wouldn't want (to treble) child allowances?" he told industrial workers last week. "But I don't think it will work. It's easy to make promises to get votes."
